function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **complete, ready‑to‑commit set of files** you can drop into the `nodejs-welcome` repository.  
I’ve kept everything in plain text so you can copy‑paste directly into your editor.

> **NOTE** – I can’t actually run `git clone`, `git add`, `git commit` or `git push` from here, but the instructions below will get you through the whole process locally.

---

## 1️⃣  Clone the repo (local machine)

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣  Analyse & create the artefacts

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the **root** of the repo:

```dockerfile
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Dockerfile for nodejs-welcome
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Use the official Node.js LTS image (Alpine for a small footprint)
FROM node:18-alpine

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install app dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> *Why this image?*  
> `node:18-alpine` is the current LTS, small, and contains everything needed to run a typical Express app.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a directory called `k8s` (or `deployments`) and inside it add a file named `deployment.yaml`:

```yaml
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# deployment.yaml – Node.js app deployment + service
# ------------------------------------------------------------
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- update with your registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> *What to change?*  
> If you’re pushing to a private registry, replace `zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest` with the full image reference (e.g. `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest`).

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions Workflow

Create the directory `.github/workflows` (if it doesn’t already exist) and add a file named `ci.yml`:

```yaml
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# .github/workflows/ci.yml – CI pipeline
# ------------------------------------------------------------
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3

      # Set up Node.js
      - name: Setup Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v3
        with:
          node-version: '18'

      # Install dependencies
      - name: Install deps
        run: npm ci

      # Run tests (optional – remove if you don’t have tests)
      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test || true

      # Build Docker image
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build -t zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .
          echo "${{ secrets.DOCKER_PASSWORD }}" | docker login -u "${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}" --password-stdin
          docker push zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}

      # Deploy to Kubernetes (requires a KUBECONFIG secret)
      - name: Deploy to K8s
        uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v1
        with:
          manifests: |
            ./k8s/deployment.yaml
          images: |
            zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
```

> **Secrets you’ll need to add in the repo settings → Secrets → Actions**  
> * `DOCKER_USERNAME` – your Docker registry username (e.g. GitHub Packages, Docker Hub, etc.)  
> * `DOCKER_PASSWORD` – the corresponding password/token  
> * `KUBECONFIG` – base64‑encoded kubeconfig if you want the workflow to deploy automatically (optional)

---

## 3️⃣  Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

If you want to keep the repo tidy, you can also add a `.gitignore` entry for the `k8s` folder if you don’t want it tracked (but usually you do want the YAMLs tracked).

---

## 4️⃣  Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

Once pushed, the GitHub Actions workflow will trigger automatically on the next push to `main`.

---

### Quick sanity check

After the push completes:

1. **Verify the Docker image** – `docker pull zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:<sha>` (replace `<sha>` with the SHA printed in the workflow logs).  
2. **Check the Kubernetes resources** – `kubectl get deployments,services -n <your-namespace>` (you should see `nodejs-welcome-deployment` and `nodejs-welcome-service`).  
3. **Test the app** – `kubectl port-forward svc/nodejs-welcome-service 8080:80` and visit `http://localhost:8080`.

That’s it! 🎉

Feel free to tweak the replica count, image tags, or test commands to suit your exact workflow.
